original_value: Humans’ activities in urban areas put a strain on local water resources. This paper introduces a method to accurately simulate the stress urban water demand in Germany puts on local resources on a single-building level, and scalable to regional levels without loss of detail. The method integrates building geometry, building physics, census, socio-economy and meteorological information to provide a general approach to assessing water demands that also overcome obstacles on data aggregation and processing imposed by data privacy guidelines. Three German counties were used as validation cases to prove the feasibility of the presented approach: on average, per capita water demand and aggregated water demand deviates by less than 7% from real demand data. Scenarios applied to a case region Ludwigsburg in Germany, which takes the increment of water price, aging of the population and the climate change into account, show that the residential water demand has the change of −2%, +7% and −0.4% respectively. The industrial water demand increases by 46% due to the development of economy indicated by GDP per capita. The rise of precipitation and temperature raise the water demand in non-residential buildings (excluding industry) of 1%.

result.paraphrase: Human activity in urban areas strains local water resources. This paper presents a method for accurately simulating the pressure that urban water demand in Germany places on local resources at single-building resolution, while remaining scalable to regional scales without losing detail. It combines building geometry, building physics, census, socio-economic, and meteorological data to offer a general framework for evaluating water demand and to overcome data aggregation and processing barriers imposed by data privacy rules. Three German counties served as validation cases, demonstrating the approach’s feasibility: on average, per-capita water demand and total water demand deviate by less than 7% from actual demand data. Scenarios for the Ludwigsburg case region in Germany, accounting for higher water prices, population aging, and climate change, indicate residential water demand changes of −2%, +7%, and −0.4%, respectively. Industrial water demand rises by 46% because of economic development as reflected by GDP per capita. Increased precipitation and temperature raise water demand in non-residential buildings excluding industry by 1%.
